newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOREIGN TRADE ON HUNGARY FUTURES A LONG-TERM BOON.
newsitem.headline: FOREIGN TRADE ON HUNGARY FUTURES A LONG-TERM BOON.

text.p: The Hungarian central bank's decision to let foreigners trade in futures of the Budapest Stock Exchange BUX index should help the market long term, traders and other analysts said.

The National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) approval goes into effect on September 30, making the Budapest bourse the first in the region, apart from the Austria Futures and Options Exchange (OTOB), to open futures trading for foreigners.
"The measure will definitely have a positive impact, the question is when," said Attila Berecz, floor trader at Raiffeisen Securities.

"If a market is opened to someone the number of market participants will rise and this is good, but I think foreigners will be cautious," said Berecz, who was one of several analysts who mentioned the BSE's continuing liquidity and settlement problems as an obstacle.

"Even if I don't have an index fund but buy (shares) of the four biggest companies in the BUX index basket, this is a good (tool) to hedge," said Gabor Sitanyi, London-based analyst for ING Barings. "But liquidity is key because without liquidity this isn't really that good an instrument."
Market participants said that at the outset the prestige value will surpass the actual impact, although in the longer term it will help to reduce the market's volatility.
"It's very important from a prestige point of view," Sitanyi said. "I would compare it to when Hungary is put into a Morgan Stanley index."
The stock exchange said the change had been essential to give a boost to the one-and-a-half-year old futures market on the Budapest bourse and to help reduce the market's volatility.

"We regard this a very important step...because foreigners come to the spot market if they can cover themselves on the futures market, at least in a certain proportion," Nora Szeles, head of the market development department of the BSE, said.
"Even if it does not have an impact immediately, hopefully it will this year," she said.
"Bigger clients will come with the aim of hedging, but there will be a good many who will speculate," she added.
